newsitem.title: JORDAN: Israel and Iraq set to dominate Jordan-U.S. talks.
newsitem.headline: Israel and Iraq set to dominate Jordan-U.S. talks.

text.p: King Hussein of Jordan heads for the White House on Tuesday for talks with President Bill Clinton overshadowed by escalating Arab-Israeli hostility and a potential row over U.S. policy towards Iraq.

Jordanian officials said the king would reiterate his firm support for peace with Israel despite a recent war of words with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the shooting of seven Israeli schoolgirls by a Jordanian soldier.

But he would warn that Israeli policies which have angered Palestinians, including Jewish settlement building in East Jerusalem and limited withdrawal from the West Bank, were also undermining Jordan's own peace treaty with Israel.
"The king was angry and is still angry at the policies of the Israeli government," a Jordanian former minister said.
"We are observing our treaty, we are trying to fulfill our treaty," he said. "But the degree of implementation will be affected by the implementation of the Palestinian accord."

The king has won debt forgiveness and military aid from the United States worth almost one billion dollars since leading Jordan into its 1994 peace treaty with Israel and steering away from his former ally President Saddam Hussein of Iraq.

But his new Prime Minister Abdul-Salam al-Majali, who flew to join him in the United States on Thursday, broke ranks on Saturday by criticising U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright's "hardline" policy statement on Iraq.

Majali, who was appointed by the king two weeks ago and enjoys good relations with Baghdad, said Albright was meddling in Iraqi affairs by suggesting her country would only deal with a post-Saddam Iraq.

He said Jordan found it "unacceptable for a country, however big or small, to interfere in the internal matters of another." Albright's comments were likely to backfire and strengthen support for Saddam, he said.
Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz said in Amman last week he welcomed Majali's appointment and spoke of "artificial tensions" with Jordan under Majali's predecessor, Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti.

Amman has played down talk of policy change towards Iraq in response to the start of the U.N. oil-for-food deal, which has eased sanction-hit Baghdad's financial crisis and sent Jordanian companies scrambling to sell goods to Iraq.

But diplomats say Jordan is worried that having turned against Saddam two years ago, King Hussein could be left exposed if U.S.-led international isolation of Baghdad, imposed after its 1990 invasion of Kuwait, starts to crumble.
"They're concerned about the state of drift in U.S. policy -- they thought Saddam would disappear and he hasn't," one Western diplomat said.
With U.S. oil companies already buying Iraqi oil under the U.N.-monitored deal, few Jordanians believe that Washington can maintain its tough anti-Iraq line indefinitely.

"The king will say (to Clinton) : 'What do you really want from Iraq?'" said a pro-government MP. "I don't consider (Albright's) statements really constitute U.S. policy over the next four years -- it is under study and it might change."
Majali has said that U.S. aid for Jordan, underpinning Amman's close support for Washington's Middle East agenda, would also be discussed at King Hussein's Tuesday talks with Clinton.

The United States wrote off Jordanian debt in 1994 and 1995 worth $630 million and has promised a $200 million squadron of fighter jets by next year. In December it delivered military equipment worth another $100 million.
But Majali said Jordanians had yet to see the fruits of their peace treaty, the much-promised "peace dividend".
